content.title: Rebuttal on major concerns proposed by the reviewer
content.comment:
We appreciate the criticisms from reviewer 6Hax, and while we disagree with three criticisms in particular, as detailed below, we are grateful for your highlighting these critical issues and making us realise we need to improve our explanations to mitigate these sorts of misunderstandings.  Since your comments are the most critical of the reviewers, we have made some changes to our paper and resubmitted to explain why your criticisms are wrong. The original comment from the reviewer are put in double quotations.

“In light of this extensive prior art, it is not clear that the first two claimed contributions of the paper offer a particularly original perspective.”

This prior art is common knowledge. Our first two claims, however, are presented entirely in the context of NER, for which our claims are original because the use of AUC with NER has not previously been explored.  Furthermore, our application to NER is only significant because the results are outstanding, so regardless of the existing use of AUC elsewhere, it is important to the NER community.

We believe the reviewer’s misconceptions about our claims may stem from the wording in our introduction “Unfortunately, most recent practical AUC surrogate loss/objective functions are solely designed to solve the binary classification task, so are not directly applicable to NER.”  Please note the use of the word “practical”.   We do not consider the OVO multiclass variant of AUC practical for its training time of each binary classifier to completion, and we found no software supporting its use in practical systems.  Hence we excluded it and provided a practical solution to the NER problem.  

We have thus added mention of OVO theory in several places, and the theory of Yang, Xu, Bao, Cao, Huang (IEEE PAMI 2021) is most advanced. 

“Once it is considered as a label classification problem, it is unclear that there is anything in the NER task that requires any specific and novel mechanism beyond straightforward applications of well-known classification methods.”

One of the experiments we ran for sentence classification, but didn’t include in the paper due to space, was testing the hypothesis that maybe the effect was mainly due to imbalanced classes and not intrinsically due to the NER problem.  In these tests, we discovered the same substantial small sample improvement was not obtained with AUC on imbalanced classes.  Thus we concluded the NER problem has some intrinsic differences.  Hence we disagree with your opinion.

“the third contribution, I found the Bayesian interpretation of AUC maximization obscure and unconvincing.”

We are perplexed by this opinion.  Allow us to highlight the role of our Bayesian contribution in the context of current consistency theory for AUC, which you haven't mentioned but we assume you are aware of.  Our Lemma 2 can be used to reproduce the consistency theory of Gao and Zhou 2015 (and echoed for the multiclass OVO case by Yang, Xu, Bao, Cao, Huang 2021), but does so more directly and with a lot less complexity and less proof.  Instead of building an interpretation of consistency and theory for it, and then developing surrogate losses specifically to match the consistency interpretation, our method piggy-backs on the existing well developed theory of strictly proper scoring rules, Gneiting & Raftery (2007), a fundamental theory for all supervised classification.  We only need to prove that the Bayes optimal classifier optimises AUC.  Once this is done, all strictly proper scoring rules become consistent automatically.  That is, results equivalent to their surrogate loss consistency fall out by the theory of strictly proper scoring rules. Our theorem also shows, surprisingly, the same result holds for the finite sample case of an optimal posterior Bayesian classifier (the classifier using Bayesian posterior expected probabilities).  

These together are original, fundamental results that substantially simplify existing AUC theory.  We strengthened Section 3.2 to highlight this.

content.title: Rebuttal on major concerns proposed by the reviewer
content.comment:
We appreciate the constructive feedback that reviewer xWfy has given and hope to resolve the questions you have for our paper via our official comment. The original comments from the reviewer are put in double quotations.

“One concern is that the computation cost is much larger than the traditional sequence labeling models, the speed should be evaluated. Also, the one-vs-all model trained the model separately, then the label dependency (e.g. I-ORG should follow B-ORG) can not be used in the prediction. This information loss will affect the model's performance.”

We are delighted that reviewer xWfy has given his/her input on this computational issue, which is one of the problems that we tried to address under our OVA frameworks.  Regarding the computational issue, we included the running time of both the baselines and our techniques in table 6 in the appendix. This table suggests that while it is true that our techniques generally double the time compared to CE, this might not be the case when our techniques are compared with CRF. Furthermore, we also believe that since our main objective is to deal with the low-resource situation, time should not be the primary objective as when you don’t have sufficient data, having techniques that have a better running time but give poor results would not be beneficial in a real-world scenario.

Moreover, while it is true that the reviewer correctly pointed out that our techniques disregard the label dependency which can serve as an important input to generate the final label prediction, this is also the case for the traditional NER models trained with the Cross Entropy loss (CE). Given that many of the state-of-the-art NER works use the CE loss to train their model, they do ignore this label dependency as well.  It is a challenging problem that we would like to address in future.

“The paper is not well organized, some details should be more clear in this paper, e.g. "We group the binary classifiers for labels that share similar linguistic characteristics (e.g., B-PER, B-ORG, B-MISC and B-LOC for CoNLL 2003) and train their classifiers together" this statement is confusing, is it binary classification or not? If yes, how do you combine them together?”

We appreciated the constructive feedback regarding the clearness of writing and hope to make amendments to this issue in the final print. Regarding the reviewer’s question, for our OVA-AUC method, we:

1. Create multiple binary classifiers for each class, says CoNLL 2003 with 9 classes, then we will create 9 binary classifiers.
2. Have one group for all classifiers starting with B, another group for all classifiers starting with I together, and the last group for the O classifier.
3. Train each group independently

By grouping, we mean that we will construct the loss of each classifier based on equation 1 and add the losses of classifiers in the same group together, i.e., loss_B = loss_B-ORG + loss_B-PER + loss_B-MISC + loss_B-LOC, with each of the losses, e.g., loss_B-ORG, will be constructed by equation 1. This process is reflected in our Algorithm 1 in the appendix.

content.title: Rebuttal on major concerns proposed by the reviewer
content.comment:
We are delighted that reviewer H8Rr has given many praises to our work and hope to resolve the remaining questions that you might have for our paper. The original comments from the reviewer are put in double quotations.

“The authors admitted that one main drawback of OVA is that training multiple binary classifiers could be time consuming. For NER tasks, if we build a set of classifiers {B-entity_type_1, I-entity_type_2, O} for each entity type, the number of classifiers could be large when the number of entity types becomes large. I am wondering if there is any remedy solution to alleviate this problem? Is it possible to build entity_type agnostic classifiers that conditioned on entity types such that only three classifiers are needed. I pretty much appreciate if the authors can share their thoughts on this.”

The issue of high training time as both you and reviewer xWfy aptly emphasised were indeed one of the main hurdles. While it is true that our techniques could reduce the training time to such an extent that we might only cost twice the amount of time the model trained with CE takes (shown in table 6 in the appendix), there might still be some room for improvements. Such improvements should be possible via focusing on our OVA-AUC-MAML.  This technique not only gives competitive performance in the low-resource setting but also has comparable training time to CRF when longer sentences are involved (e.g., Ontonotes 5). Since our OVA-AUC-MAML is based on the original work which was published in 2017 (Finn et al., 2017), there has been numerous state-of-the-art works focusing on fine-tuning the meta-learning strategy to improve both the performance and the speed of convergence, e.g., designing an adaptive task scheduler to focus on which classifier should be trained in each iteration (Yao et al., 2021). 

The idea of having entity type agnostic classifiers that are conditioned on entity types is worth exploring and there are possibly other hierarchical structured classification techniques in machine learning that could be used. However, we believe that this is mostly subject to our future work since such a problem would require an in-depth reformulation of the NER problem.

“On page 4, the paragraph below eq(2), the authors claimed "AUC maximization can lead to well-tuned binary classifiers ... weakness should be naturally mitigated". Can you elaborate more about why the weakness is naturally mitigated? or do we have evidence to support it?”

For the claim that the AUC maximization can lead to well-tuned binary classifiers, we hope that our subsection 5.3 would present enough evidence to support this claim where the binary classifiers trained with OVA-AUC having fewer predictions in the confusion area compared to ones trained with cross entropy. For the “weakness should be naturally mitigated”, the “weakness” we were trying to address is one of the weaknesses that Liu et al., 2017b proposed as the natural problem of OVA setup: uneven data distribution leads to degraded performance of the binary classifiers. By “naturally mitigated”, we were based on the claim of Gao et al. (2013) and Ying et al. (2016) that AUC optimization should be the optimal solution for imbalance/uneven data distribution problem.

Having said that, we appreciated the constructive feedback and will make the necessary modifications to our paper to communicate our intents clearer.

“To demonstrate the advantage of proposed methods under low-resource settings, all training datasets are small. I assume the time cost would increases significantly when training size increase. I am still interested in the feasibility to experiment on larger size dataset. And how it performances when compared to other SOTA NER approaches.”

We have run some additional test to verify the performance of both the baselines and our techniques on full training dataset for CoNLL 2003 which contains 14,040 sentences, the results are as follows: The F1-result for CE is 0.9204 with runtime of 2,171 seconds, the F1-result for CRF is 0.8483 with runtime of 2,459 seconds, and the F1-result for our OVA-AUC-MAML is 0.9185 with runtime of 2,980 seconds.  These runtime are collected from the whole training phase. From these results, it is not surprising that there is a lack of improvements since asymptotically, maximum likelihood solutions will produce the best results and special purpose loss such as AUC should only be substantial in specific settings, such as the low-resource data setting that our work focuses on.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Most of existing works predominately approach NER as a multi-class classification problem which optimizes cross-entropy loss or train a CRF classifier. Despite showing effectiveness in vast of works, these objectives suffer various problems, i.e degraded performance, due to imbalanced label distributions that inherited from NER training dataset. Instead of adopting CE or CRF, this work frames NER as a one-vs-all learning problem which optimize an AUC surrogate loss to train multiple binary classifiers. This AUC maximization is able to address common limitations of OVA under imbalance settings, e.g competence among classifiers or weak classifiers with low confidence. Moreover, they interpreted their decent experiment results with AUC maximization under Bayesian theory. Extensive experiments under low-resource NER settings demonstrated the effectiveness of their method. They also conducted ablations to show their methods are robust and general framework that can be extended to other NER settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- This is a well-motivated and solid work that can benefit the whole NER community
- Formulating NER as a OVA problem with AUC surrogate loss effectively overcomes limitations of OVA, resulting in well-tuned binary classifiers for imbalanced data. 
- Interpreting AUX maximization under Bayesian theory enable their methods to be a general framework that can be applies to other NER settings.
- Extensive experiments on several public benchmarks in various experiment settings demonstrated their methods are robust to low-resource and data imbalance challenges.
- Additional ablations, e.g on imbalance data distribution and analysis confusion areas under OVA framework etc., convey interesting and inspiring findings.

Major Concerns:
- The authors admitted that one main drawback of OVA is that training multiple binary classifiers could be time consuming. For NER tasks, if we build a set of classifiers {B-entity_type_1, I-entity_type_2, O} for each entity type, the number of classifiers could be large when the number of entity types becomes large. I am wondering if there is any remedy solution to alleviate this problem? Is it possible to build entity_type agnostic classifiers that conditioned on entity types such that only three classifiers are needed. I pretty much appreciate if the authors can share their thoughts on this.
- On page 4, the paragraph below eq(2), the authors claimed "AUC maximization can lead to well-tuned binary classifiers ... weakness should be naturally mitigated". Can you elaborate more about why the weakness is naturally mitigated? or do we have evidence to support it?
- To demonstrate the advantage of proposed methods under low-resource settings, all training datasets are small. I assume the time cost would increases significantly when training size increase. content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses named entity recognition by formulating the multi class entity labelling problem as a combination of one-versus-all classifications, and training the underlying imbalanced binary classifiers using AUC maximization. A Bayesian perspective on AUC maximization is also proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Named entity recognition is definitely an interesting and highly relevant problem in NLP. The idea seems fairly straightforward and is shown empirically to be effective.

The formulation of single-label multi-class classification as a combination of one-versus-all or one-versus-one binary classification rules, and the associated issues (such as the tension between multi-label and single-label classification) has been known and practiced for a long time. Similarly, addressing class imbalance with AUC is well-known (in fact David J. Hand proposed an extension of AUC to multi-class in early 2000s). In light of this extensive prior art, it is not clear that the first two claimed contributions of the paper offer a particularly original perspective. Once it is considered as a label classification problem, it is unclear that there is anything in the NER task that requires any specific and novel mechanism beyond straightforward applications of well-known classification methods. The paper definitely does not provide evidence that NER is different from any other imbalanced multi class problem.

Re. the third contribution, I found the Bayesian interpretation of AUC maximization obscure and unconvincing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, the organization of the paper is confusing and the narrative is not very clear. Novelty was addressed in the previous paragraph. The paper relies on standard benchmarks and the proposed idea is straightforward so it is likely that similar experiments could be replicated fairly easily, although exact reproducibility would require the release of the code promised in the paper in order to match data samples and re-run the precise experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea makes sense and is empirically effective, however this is not overly surprising as the underlying ideas have been known and practiced for a long time, as shown in extensive prior art going back 20+ years.

content.title: One-Vs-All AUC Maximization: an effective solution to the low-resource named entity recognition problem
content.abstract: Named entity recognition (NER), a sequence labelling/token classification task, has been traditionally considered a multi-class classification problem, the learning objective of which is to either optimise the multi-class cross entropy loss (CE) or train a conditional random field (CRF). However, these standard learning objectives, though scalable to large NER datasets and used in state-of-the-art work, largely ignore the problem of imbalanced label distributions that is inherent in all NER corpora. We show this leads to degraded performance in low-resource settings. While reformulating this standard multi-class labelling problem as a one-vs-all (OVA) learning problem, we propose to optimise the NER model with an AUC-based alternative loss function that is more capable of handling imbalanced datasets. As OVA often leads to a higher training time compared to the standard multi-class setting, we also develop two training strategies, one trains together the labels that share similar linguistic characteristics, and another employs a meta-learning approach to speed convergence. In order to motivate some of our experiments and better interpret the results, we also develop a Bayesian theory for what is the  AUC function during learning. Experimental results under low-resource NER settings from benchmark corpora show that our methods can achieve consistently better performance compared with the learning objectives commonly used in NER. We also give evidence that our methods are robust and agnostic to the underlying NER embeddings, models, domains, and label distributions. The code to replicate this work will be released upon the publication of this paper.
